video_title: The Average Retirement Savings By Age - How Are You Doing? | Julia Lembcke
gist: CFP Julia Lemke (URS Advisory) walks Adam Taggart through 2026 Empower retirement-savings benchmarks by age (median ~$440k-$570k vs averages ~$1-1.24M) and an age-bracket checklist: diversify across pre-tax/Roth/brokerage, time Roth conversions before RMDs and in market drawdowns, coordinate ACA subsidies and Medicare IRMAA, choose Medigap vs Medicare Advantage carefully at 65, and use DAFs/QCDs and estate planning. Personal-finance episode with little market-level signal beyond boomer retirement-crisis and Medicare sustainability concerns.

insights.claim: Per a 2026 Empower survey of active 401k savers, savers aged ~55-60 have average retirement savings of about $1.02 million but a median of only about $440,000.
insights.speaker: Julia Lemke
insights.so_what: Mean is heavily skewed by multi-millionaires; median is the realistic peer benchmark for active savers.

insights.claim: Empower 2026 data shows savers aged 60-65 average about $1.185 million with a median of $540,000; ages 65-70 average $1.24 million with a median of $570,000; ages 70+ average about $1.06 million with a median of about $460,000.
insights.speaker: Julia Lemke
insights.so_what: Balances peak around 65-70 and then decline as drawdown begins, implying net outflows from retirement accounts by the oldest boomer cohorts.

insights.claim: Headline figures like 'the average person has $200,000 saved' include non-savers and are irrelevant benchmarks for active 401k contributors; peers should be filtered by age and saving behavior.
insights.speaker: Julia Lemke
insights.so_what: Use cohort-appropriate benchmarks when judging retirement readiness.
insights.quote: It's a fact, but it's not relevant to your demographic.

insights.claim: There is no fixed 'enough' number: Lemke has seen a client retire comfortably on $500,000 while clients with $10 million remain anxious, so readiness depends on burn rate rather than balance.
insights.speaker: Julia Lemke
insights.so_what: Spending footprint, not portfolio size, determines sustainability.
insights.quote: your ability to retire is not based on having a certain number.

insights.claim: Adam Taggart fears that, at the median level, the large wave of boomer retirements means a retirement crisis is brewing, since even Empower medians (skewed toward responsible savers) look thin and national numbers are far lower.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Implies more boomers working longer or becoming dependent on family/public programs, a pressure point for fiscal and labor-market dynamics.

insights.claim: Lemke says a 65-year-old with ~$550,000 saved typically also has a hefty pension, but pensions are now rare for people in their mid-50s, so the generation behind will have to rely on their own savings.
insights.speaker: Julia Lemke
insights.so_what: Shift from defined benefit to self-directed savings raises the stakes of individual planning and demand for advice.

insights.claim: Lemke's top advice for ages 20-60 is to diversify the 'tax landscape' into three buckets — pre-tax, Roth, and after-tax brokerage — so retirees can control their taxable income rather than having it dictated by all-pre-tax holdings.
insights.speaker: Julia Lemke
insights.so_what: Account-type mix creates flexibility for conversions, subsidies and bracket management later.
insights.quote: you can really sort of control your taxable income rather than having it be controlled for you, which is what happens when you're all pre-tax.

insights.claim: A couple with room left in the 22% bracket (e.g., $30,000 before hitting 24%) can have one spouse save pre-tax and the other fund a Roth 401k without jumping a bracket, hedging future tax rates.
insights.speaker: Julia Lemke
insights.so_what: Split-contribution tactic to build tax-free assets at a known marginal rate.

insights.claim: Lemke calls taxable brokerage accounts the 'unsung heroes' of retirement: no contribution limits, no age restrictions on withdrawals, loss harvesting, long-term capital gains rates, and basis withdrawals that are invisible on tax returns.
insights.speaker: Julia Lemke
insights.so_what: Taxable accounts fund the early-retirement bridge enabling Roth conversions and ACA subsidy qualification.
insights.quote: A brokerage account is like freedom to me.

insights.claim: Retirees should project their pre-tax balances forward to RMD age (73 or 75) to see what bracket RMDs will force; Lemke frequently sees married couples jump from the 12% to the 24% bracket once RMDs begin, at which point it is too late to fix.
insights.speaker: Julia Lemke
insights.so_what: Pre-RMD Roth conversions are the window to smooth lifetime tax rates and Medicare premiums.

insights.claim: The goal of Roth conversions is either to keep tax rates steady through retirement or to pay tax now at a lower rate than expected later; once RMDs start, Lemke says conversions are no longer worth it.
insights.speaker: Julia Lemke
insights.so_what: Conversion timing is concentrated in the years between retirement and RMD age.
insights.quote: Once you have to start taking RMDs, don't even bother.

insights.claim: Roth conversions should be done when markets are down, converting at a discount so the recovery happens inside the tax-free account — even if that means forgoing an ACA subsidy that year.
insights.speaker: Julia Lemke
insights.so_what: Market drawdowns are tax-planning opportunities; expect conversion activity to spike in selloffs.
insights.quote: You always want to do Roth conversions or move money to a tax-free account when the market is down

insights.claim: Lemke does not know of retail-facing tax projection software yet and suggests a paid AI tool can give a 'pretty darn good idea' of conversion strategy, while warning it could be wrong.
insights.speaker: Julia Lemke
insights.so_what: Gap in consumer tax-planning software is an opening for fintech/AI products.
insights.quote: I'm sure that there's one in the works, right? I'm sure that's going to be up next.

insights.claim: The 'widow's penalty': when a spouse dies, only Social Security falls (by about 30%) while RMDs and investment income stay, and spending is ~75% of prior, so survivors often jump from the 24% bracket to 32% or 35% by filing single.
insights.speaker: Julia Lemke
insights.so_what: Another argument for earlier Roth conversions and after-tax savings in married households.

insights.claim: Lemke never recommends converting an entire pre-tax account, because pre-tax money is useful for qualified charitable distributions and for paying ~$100,000/year long-term care costs that can be largely offset by itemized medical deductions.
insights.speaker: Julia Lemke
insights.so_what: Keep a residual IRA balance as a tax-efficient source for care and giving.

insights.claim: Under the 'rule of 55', anyone retired at 55 or later can withdraw from a 401k, 403b or 457 without penalty and with flexible amounts, but rolling it all into an IRA loses that, leaving only rigid 72(t) substantially-equal-payment withdrawals.
insights.speaker: Julia Lemke
insights.so_what: Early retirees should do a partial rollover and keep ~5 years of needed spending in the 401k.

insights.claim: Many retirees mistakenly believe they cannot touch their 401k until 59 and a half and are surprised to learn they can retire earlier and draw from it.
insights.speaker: Julia Lemke
insights.so_what: Rule awareness can accelerate retirement timing for some savers.

insights.claim: Between ages 60 and 63, an enhanced catch-up lets employer-plan participants contribute nearly $12,000 extra instead of $8,000, and in many plans that catch-up must go to the Roth 401k side.
insights.speaker: Julia Lemke
insights.so_what: Mandatory Roth catch-ups shift flows toward tax-free accounts for near-retirees.

insights.claim: RMDs are calculated by dividing the December 31 account balance of the year before (age 72 for a 73-year-old start) by an IRS factor; clients who don't need the money donate it, reinvest it in a brokerage account after tax, or gift it to kids/grandkids.
insights.speaker: Julia Lemke
insights.so_what: RMD-driven reinvestment and gifting is a steady flow out of tax-deferred accounts.

insights.claim: Lemke stress-tests pre-Medicare retirement by assuming full-price ACA coverage of ~$1,500/month ($18,000/year) inflating at 5-7% annually; if the plan absorbs that, healthcare is a psychological fear, not a financial reason to delay retirement.
insights.speaker: Julia Lemke
insights.so_what: Healthcare inflation of 5-7% is the planning assumption; worst-case modeling unlocks earlier retirement.
insights.quote: That's not a financial risk. That's just a psychological fear.

insights.claim: Five pre-Medicare healthcare options are: worst-case full-price ACA, joining a working spouse's plan, COBRA for 18 months, short-term catastrophic coverage within a year of Medicare, and controlling income (e.g., living on brokerage basis) to qualify for ACA premium subsidies.
insights.speaker: Julia Lemke
insights.so_what: Income control via account mix directly lowers healthcare costs.

insights.claim: ACA subsidy eligibility for married filing jointly requires keeping income under roughly $80,000, while the 2026 Medicare IRMAA threshold for joint filers is about $218,000 with a two-year lookback, so Roth conversions can be deferred to after 65 when there is more room.
insights.speaker: Julia Lemke
insights.so_what: Coordinate conversion timing with healthcare subsidy thresholds.

insights.claim: HSA funds cannot pay most Medicare premiums but can pay ACA premiums; savers can also bank medical receipts for decades and reimburse themselves later, since an inherited HSA is taxed to beneficiaries immediately.
insights.speaker: Julia Lemke
insights.so_what: HSAs are best spent down by the owner rather than left as an inheritance.

insights.claim: Medicare Advantage plans have near-zero premiums but restrict networks, require referrals and prior authorization, while Medigap/Medicare supplements cost a few hundred dollars a month but let doctors direct care nationwide; Lemke prefers supplements, though quality varies by state.
insights.speaker: Julia Lemke
insights.so_what: Insurer-run Advantage plans control care via networks and approvals — relevant to managed-care economics.

insights.claim: Seniors can join any Medicare supplement without health questions only during the initial six-month enrollment window; afterwards they must pass underwriting, which keeps supplement premiums down and can trap unhealthy retirees in Medicare Advantage.
insights.speaker: Julia Lemke
insights.so_what: Initial plan choice at 65 is effectively irreversible for many, locking in Advantage enrollment.
insights.quote: You are stuck on an advantage plan.

insights.claim: Total Medicare costs can reach about $12,000 a year at the top (Part B premiums ranging from about $200 to $700/month by income, plus supplement and drug plans), with an average around $600 a month.
insights.speaker: Julia Lemke
insights.so_what: Income-related premiums are a tax-like cost to manage in retirement.

insights.claim: Taggart says his mother received what he estimates as millions of dollars of care on a Medicare Advantage plan while paying nothing, which he views as fiscally unsustainable from a taxpayer's perspective.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Signals political/fiscal pressure on Medicare spending.
insights.quote: there's no way that's fiscally sustainable.

insights.claim: Lemke moved $250,000 of a client's most highly appreciated company stock (RSU-derived, low basis) into a donor advised fund to cover 13 years of tithing, avoiding capital gains, diversifying concentration risk, and creating a deduction large enough to do a $100,000 Roth conversion at 12%.
insights.speaker: Julia Lemke
insights.so_what: Pairing DAF contributions with conversions is a powerful tax-neutralizing move for concentrated stockholders.

insights.claim: From age 70 and a half, qualified charitable distributions let IRA owners give directly to 501(c)(3) charities tax-free (Lemke cites about $108,000 per person this year), reducing RMDs dollar for dollar; it is the most tax-efficient way to give but not available from a 401k.
insights.speaker: Julia Lemke
insights.so_what: Large givers should front-load QCDs in January to cut RMD taxable income.
insights.quote: That is the most tax-efficient way to give to charity is through a qualified charitable distribution

insights.claim: In forensic spending reviews, most clients discover they spend about 15-20% more than they thought, and spending typically jumps early in retirement on travel and home renovations.
insights.speaker: Julia Lemke
insights.so_what: Budget a cushion; underestimated burn rates are the main risk to retirement sustainability.

insights.claim: Lemke advises holding about five years of living expenses outside stocks so retirees aren't forced to sell when markets crash, giving the market time to recover.
insights.speaker: Julia Lemke
insights.so_what: Bucket strategy reduces sequence-of-returns risk.
insights.quote: I have my five years of living expenses and it gives the market time to recover.

insights.claim: Deliberately spending down or gifting assets to qualify for Medicaid is not a real strategy: qualifying assets are about $2,000 plus a home, there is a five-year lookback, and starting care as a Medicaid patient sharply limits facility options.
insights.speaker: Julia Lemke
insights.so_what: Plan to self-fund long-term care (~$100,000/year) before any Medicaid transition.
insights.quote: You want to start off being a paid client or patient and then transfer to Medicaid.

insights.claim: Revocable living trusts avoid probate, stay private, and let grantors attach conditions (e.g., age or graduation) to inheritances, protecting spendthrift heirs.
insights.speaker: Julia Lemke
insights.so_what: Estate structuring lowers friction and legal costs in wealth transfer.
